meta.blurb: Every day at three, Hana's energy vanishes, and coffee and a biscuit do not fix it. Her colleague Dev, a part-time running coach, helps her test sleep, light, meals and movement, and tells her what is proven and what is not.
meta.bible: Hana: an office worker of about thirty-five whose energy drops every afternoon; practical, tired and funny. Dev: her colleague, a part-time running Coach who reads about health; calm, encouraging and careful to say what is proven and what is not. The story runs over about four weeks in a busy office, a park and Hana's flat. Key terms: Energy, Calories, Cells, Body clock, Circadian rhythm, Daylight, Adenosine, Caffeine, Blood sugar, Glucose, Insulin, Fibre, Protein, Whole grains, Glycaemic index, Dehydration, Iron, Vitamin B12, Vitamin D, Diabetes, Glucose monitor, Adrenal fatigue, Registered dietitian. Facts: the body turns food and oxygen into usable energy inside every cell; the afternoon dip in alertness is partly driven by the body clock and happens even without lunch; adults are usually advised to sleep at least seven hours; caffeine blocks the brain's sleepiness signal, can stay in the body for many hours, and for most adults up to about four cups of coffee a day is considered safe, and less in pregnancy; blood sugar rises after meals in every healthy person and the body brings it back down with insulin; fibre, protein and fat slow digestion; several small trials found that a short walk after a meal lowers the rise in blood sugar; regular exercise reduces tiredness in trials; adrenal fatigue is not a recognised medical condition; alcohol can help people fall asleep but harms the quality of sleep. Foods: Oats, Beans, Lentils, Eggs, Yoghurt, Nuts, Fruit, Vegetables, Wholemeal bread, Brown rice, Coffee, Tea, Water. Safety facts: tiredness that lasts for weeks, or comes with extreme thirst, frequent urination, blurred vision, unexplained weight loss, low mood or breathlessness, needs a doctor and not a diet; people with diabetes, a pregnancy, a child to feed or on medicine should follow their doctor's advice and ask a doctor or registered dietitian before changing their diet; do not take iron pills unless a doctor advises it. This book is general information and is not medical advice. Added for the full-length book: Marcus: Hana's manager; his Tuesday team meeting at three fifteen is moved to eleven. Priya: Hana's neighbour at the next desk, drinks energy drinks, takes iron tablets without a test until Dev asks her to see a doctor, tries water and tea for a week; her brother is a nurse on night shifts. Nina and Sam: Hana's friends at the picnic. Leila: Hana's sister, with a newborn baby. Aunt Ruth: Dev's aunt, who lives with a long illness that makes her tired every day. Timeline: four weeks; week one covers the diary, the body clock, morning light and sleep; later weeks cover coffee, blood sugar, meals, water, snacks, cooking, vitamins, movement, stress, evenings, myths, the doctor and the review. Hana's doctor's blood test comes back normal. Dev labels every claim proven, likely or unknown. More facts used: the brain uses about a fifth of the body's energy; the body stores energy in the liver, muscles and fat; many parts of the body have clocks kept in time by a master clock in the brain; in studies where people were kept from eating the early afternoon dip still came; adenosine builds up while awake and caffeine blocks the signal; about half of a dose of caffeine is still in the body after about five hours in the average adult but this varies a great deal; stopping caffeine suddenly can cause a headache for a few days; insulin moves glucose into cells; the glycaemic index is only a rough guide; a short walk after a meal lowered the blood sugar rise in several small trials; eating vegetables and protein first is early evidence only; adults are advised about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week and strengthening activity at least twice a week; moderate means you can talk but not sing; iron helps blood carry oxygen and low iron is a common cause of tiredness found by a blood test; vitamin B12 comes mainly from animal foods and people who eat none are advised fortified foods or a supplement; sunlight helps the skin make vitamin D and some countries advise a supplement in winter; vitamins give no extra energy unless the body is short of them; energy drinks are not advised for children; glucose monitors help people with diabetes and have unclear benefit for healthy people; sleep trackers give estimates; a warm bath an hour or two before bed may help some people fall asleep and the effect is small; a study that shows two things are linked does not show that one causes the other; real adrenal disease exists but is rare and is not adrenal fatigue; warning signs for a doctor are tiredness for weeks, extreme thirst, passing urine very often, blurred vision, unexplained weight loss, breathlessness and low mood; some medicines cause drowsiness and must not be stopped without asking a doctor or pharmacist. Voice and tone: warm, clear and a little funny; honest about uncertainty; no invented numbers, studies or quotes; no diagnosis and no personal treatment advice.
chapters: Sugar Goes Up, Sugar Comes Down
Stress, Breaks and the Tired Mind

beats.scene: Hana yawns at her office desk at three o'clock beside an empty coffee cup
beats.summary: At three o'clock every afternoon Hana's energy disappears, and she reaches for coffee and a biscuit.

beats.scene: Hana stares at a blurry spreadsheet beneath a clock showing ten past three
beats.summary: At ten past three the numbers on her screen begin to swim, and her manager Marcus glances over with a worried look.

beats.scene: Dev laces his running shoes beside a desk covered in running magazines
beats.summary: Her colleague Dev, a part-time running coach who reads about health, notices her struggle and offers to help.

beats.scene: Hana pins a note to her screen, and Dev writes three words beside it
beats.summary: Dev promises to label every claim as proven, likely or unknown, so Hana always knows how strong the evidence is.

beats.scene: Hana counts three half-empty tea boxes and a bottle of tablets on her shelf
beats.summary: Hana admits that she has already tried miracle teas, tablets and a juice cleanse, and none of them lasted.

beats.scene: Hana and Dev shake hands over a calendar with four weeks circled
beats.summary: They agree on a four-week experiment in which Hana changes one habit at a time and watches what happens.

beats.scene: Hana opens a new notebook and draws three columns at her desk
beats.summary: Hana starts an energy diary, scoring her energy from one to ten three times a day.

beats.scene: Hana's first diary page shows low scores and a coffee ring
beats.summary: Her first day shows the baseline: a short night, three coffees, a skipped lunch and a very low score at three.

beats.scene: Dev gives Hana a small card with a doctor's name on it
beats.summary: Dev warns that one person's result is not proof, and that long, heavy tiredness should be checked by a doctor first.

beats.scene: Hana sits up in bed with a lamp and a notebook
beats.summary: That evening Hana feels hopeful for the first time in months and decides to start properly the next morning.

beats.scene: Dev draws a simple cell with a tiny lightning bolt on a notepad
beats.summary: Every cell turns food and oxygen into usable energy, and Dev says that this is the heart of the whole subject.

beats.scene: A biscuit packet turned over to show a table of numbers
beats.summary: Calories are a measure of the energy in food, and a food label is simply a measuring tape.

beats.scene: A heart, lungs and a thermometer drawn on a notepad
beats.summary: Most of the body's energy goes into staying alive, by keeping the heart beating, the lungs working and the body warm.

beats.scene: A drawing of a head with a glowing brain and a pie chart
beats.summary: The brain is small, yet it uses about a fifth of the body's energy, so thinking really does cost fuel.

beats.scene: Hana studies a drawing of a tired face with three question marks
beats.summary: Dev explains that feeling tired is a signal made from many things, including sleep, mood, food and health, not just calories.

beats.scene: Hana takes a slow deep breath beside an open window
beats.summary: Oxygen matters as much as food, and the blood carries it from the lungs to every cell.

beats.scene: Dev draws three faces labelled sleepy, body-tired and mind-tired
beats.summary: Dev says that tiredness comes in three kinds, sleepiness, tired muscles and a tired mind, and each needs its own remedy.

beats.scene: A body outline showing a liver, muscles and a small pile of fat
beats.summary: The body stores energy in the liver, in muscles and as fat, so it does not run like a car with a tiny tank.

beats.scene: Hana looks puzzled with a pen at her lips beside a plate
beats.summary: Hana asks whether she simply needs more calories, and Dev answers that eating too little and too much can both drain energy.

beats.scene: Priya peers over a screen at Hana's notebook, holding an energy drink can
beats.summary: Hana's neighbour Priya spots the diary and says she lives on energy drinks, so Dev adds her to his list of things to examine.

beats.scene: A large wall clock in the office with a sun rising in its face
beats.summary: The body has a clock of about twenty-four hours, and it makes us more alert at some times and sleepier at others.

beats.scene: A glowing dot in a drawn head, with tiny clocks on each organ
beats.summary: One master clock in the brain keeps time for many smaller clocks in other parts of the body.

beats.scene: A wavy line rising to a peak at noon and falling at three
beats.summary: Alertness rises through the morning, peaks near midday and dips in the early afternoon, in a gentle daily wave.

beats.scene: An empty lunch tray beside a laboratory clock and a yawning volunteer
beats.summary: In studies where people were kept from eating, the early afternoon dip still arrived, so lunch cannot be the only cause.

beats.scene: Dev, wide awake at dawn, stands beside Hana, who is hiding under a blanket
beats.summary: People differ in their natural timing: some are larks who wake early, some are owls who stay up late, and genes play a part.

beats.scene: A meeting-room calendar entry reading three fifteen every Tuesday
beats.summary: Marcus's Tuesday team meeting falls at the very hour of Hana's deepest dip, which turns out to be a poor time to think hard.

beats.scene: Hana writes hard tasks in a morning column and easy tasks in another
beats.summary: Hana moves her hardest work to late morning, when she is sharpest, and keeps simple emails for the afternoon.

beats.scene: Priya's brother in a hospital uniform walks home at dawn
beats.summary: Priya's brother works night shifts, which push the body clock out of step with the sun, and Dev says that this is truly hard on energy.

beats.scene: A calendar with a bedtime circled each night and a sleeping figure on Saturday
beats.summary: A steady routine helps the clock, and sleeping very late at weekends can shift it, which people call social jet lag.

beats.scene: Hana looks at a diary page headed with a small wave
beats.summary: By the third day Hana still feels the afternoon dip, but now she knows that it is a wave from her clock and not a fault.

beats.scene: Sunlight pours through a bedroom window onto a half-open curtain
beats.summary: Light is the strongest signal that tells the body clock that the day has begun.

beats.scene: Hana steps off a bus one stop early near a leafy park
beats.summary: Hana starts getting off the bus a stop early so that she can walk in the morning light.

beats.scene: A bright sky outside a window and a dim ceiling lamp inside
beats.summary: Even on a cloudy day the light outdoors is far stronger than the light inside an office.

beats.scene: Hana's desk beside a window with the blinds pulled up
beats.summary: Hana asks Marcus if she can move her desk to the window, and he agrees with a shrug and a smile.

beats.scene: A wall chart comparing a bright morning with a dim late evening
beats.summary: Dev says that morning light helps to set the body clock, but how much it improves a person's energy is less certain.

beats.scene: Hana pulls back her bedroom curtains and squints in the early light
beats.summary: Hana opens her curtains the minute her alarm rings, and she finds it easier to leave her bed.

beats.scene: A frosty street at eight in the morning with a lamp still lit
beats.summary: In the dark months it is harder to get light, so a lunchtime walk matters more, and a doctor can advise on bright-light lamps.

beats.scene: A hat, sunscreen and sunglasses laid out on a park bench
beats.summary: Dev reminds her never to look at the sun, and to protect her skin when the sun is strong.

beats.scene: Hana studies a diary page with a row of morning scores circled
beats.summary: After four days of morning walks Hana's mornings score higher on bright days, although her afternoons barely change.

beats.scene: Dev raises a thumb beside Hana's diary in a sunlit office kitchen
beats.summary: Dev says that a mixed result is still a result, and that the experiment is working because it shows what does not help.

beats.scene: A dark bedroom with a clock showing eleven and a lamp switched off
beats.summary: Adults are usually advised to sleep at least seven hours a night, and sleep is the base of daytime energy.

beats.scene: Hana counts on her fingers beside a clock reading half past midnight
beats.summary: Hana counts her real sleep and finds that she gets about six hours, not seven, on most nights.

beats.scene: A plate of biscuits and crisps beside a yawning person at a night desk
beats.summary: After short sleep people tend to feel hungrier and crave sweet food, so poor sleep can look like a food problem.

beats.scene: A drawn wave with steps going down and up through the night
beats.summary: Sleep moves through light and deep stages in cycles of about an hour and a half, and each cycle does different work.

beats.scene: A sofa with a pillow and a crumpled blanket on a Sunday morning
beats.summary: A long weekend lie-in repays only part of a week's lost sleep, and the evidence about catching up is mixed.

beats.scene: Hana's phone showing a bedtime alarm at half past ten
beats.summary: Hana sets a bedtime reminder for half past ten, and treats it like an appointment she must keep.

beats.scene: Hana lies in bed on Saturday morning with the alarm clock ringing
beats.summary: Hana wakes at the same time on Saturday and Sunday as on work days, and is grumpy for a day, then glad.

beats.scene: A sleeper with a loud open mouth beside a worried partner
beats.summary: Loud snoring with gasps, or feeling tired after a full night, may be a sleeping disorder, and Dev says that it needs a doctor.

beats.scene: Hana sits in a chair by a lamp with a book
beats.summary: If she lies awake for a long time, Hana gets up and does something quiet, and a long-lasting problem with sleep needs a doctor.

beats.scene: Hana studies a diary with an upward arrow beside the number seven
beats.summary: At the end of the first week, after a few nights of seven hours, Hana's dip at three is smaller, though not gone, and Dev refuses to oversell the result.

beats.scene: A row of mugs with a stack of receipts from a coffee shop
beats.summary: Hana admits that she drinks three coffees and a fizzy cola every working day.

beats.scene: A coffee cup and a small drawing of a sleepy brain signal being blocked
beats.summary: Through the day a chemical called adenosine builds up and makes us sleepy, and caffeine blocks the signal.

beats.scene: A mug in front of a blanket laid over a heap of tired signals
beats.summary: Dev says that caffeine does not make energy; it hides tiredness for a while, and the tiredness is still there.

beats.scene: A drawing of a coffee cup with a long fading tail of hours
beats.summary: Caffeine takes many hours to leave the body, about five hours for the average adult, though it varies a great deal.

beats.scene: Hana stops at a tea kiosk and waves away an afternoon coffee
beats.summary: Hana moves her coffee to the morning and stops drinking it after lunch to protect her sleep.

beats.scene: A pregnant woman holds a decaf cup beside a doctor's leaflet
beats.summary: For most adults up to about four cups of coffee a day is considered safe, but pregnant people are advised to have less.

beats.scene: Hana holds her head at her desk with a cup of water beside her
beats.summary: When Hana cuts coffee down suddenly she gets a headache and feels sluggish, which Dev says is common for a few days.

beats.scene: A tea bag, a can of cola and dark chocolate on a table
beats.summary: Tea, cola and chocolate also contain caffeine, and even decaffeinated coffee has a small amount.

beats.scene: A hand shaking slightly beside a coffee cup and a fast heartbeat line
beats.summary: Some people feel jittery or notice a racing heart after caffeine, and anyone who worries about it should ask a doctor.

beats.scene: Hana circles two diary entries beside a mug with a small sun
beats.summary: After four days of morning-only coffee, Hana sleeps better and her afternoons are slightly steadier, though she misses her three o'clock cup.

beats.scene: A diagram of a slice of bread turning into sugar cubes in the blood
beats.summary: Carbohydrates are broken down into glucose, the sugar in the blood, which the body uses as fuel.

beats.scene: A brain drawn beside a bowl of rice and a lightning bolt
beats.summary: Glucose is the body's main fuel and the brain depends on it, so a steady supply matters.

beats.scene: Dev draws a tiny key opening the door of a cell
beats.summary: The hormone insulin acts like a key that moves glucose from the blood into the cells.

beats.scene: A gentle wave line rises after a meal and falls on a graph
beats.summary: Blood sugar rises after every meal in every healthy person and then falls; this rise and fall is normal.

beats.scene: A tall glass of sweet juice next to a bowl of lentils
beats.summary: Foods that are digested quickly, such as sugary drinks and white bread, raise blood sugar faster than foods rich in fibre.

beats.scene: A chart with a label, glycaemic index, and a ladder of foods
beats.summary: The glycaemic index ranks foods by how fast they raise blood sugar, but it is only a rough guide.

beats.scene: A balanced plate with brown rice, beans, fish and a green salad
beats.summary: Fibre, protein and fat slow digestion, so a balanced meal raises blood sugar more gently.

beats.scene: Hana eats white toast one morning and egg on toast the next morning
beats.summary: Hana tests plain toast against toast with an egg and feels fuller after the egg, but Dev reminds her that one test proves little.

beats.scene: A tired person with a plate of sweets and a rollercoaster graph
beats.summary: A large swing in blood sugar may make some people feel tired, but the evidence is mixed and the dip happens without it.

beats.scene: A thermostat beside a drawing of a steady line with a narrow band
beats.summary: The healthy body keeps blood sugar within a narrow range, and in diabetes that control fails, which is why it needs medical care.

beats.scene: A loaf of wholemeal bread beside a jar of oats and beans
beats.summary: Whole grains and beans digest slowly and keep their fibre, so they are better for steady energy than refined grains.

beats.scene: A grain of wheat cut in layers beside a slice of white bread
beats.summary: A whole grain keeps its outer layer and its germ, while white flour has lost most of them, and the fibre goes with them.

beats.scene: A tin of beans, a bag of lentils and a pot of chickpeas
beats.summary: Beans and lentils give fibre, protein and iron at a low price, which makes them a hero of the steady plate.

beats.scene: A freezer drawer full of bags of peas, spinach and broccoli
beats.summary: Vegetables fill half the plate, and frozen or tinned ones count just as well as fresh ones.

beats.scene: Eggs, fish, yoghurt, tofu and chicken laid out in a row
beats.summary: Protein from eggs, fish, yoghurt, tofu, beans or meat slows digestion and helps people to feel full.

beats.scene: A bowl of nuts, olive oil and an avocado on a counter
beats.summary: Healthy fats such as nuts, olive oil and avocado are not the enemy, and they slow digestion as well.

beats.scene: A plate divided into three sections with vegetables, grains and protein
beats.summary: A steady plate: about half vegetables and fruit, a quarter whole grains or starchy foods, and a quarter protein.

beats.scene: A plate where vegetables sit first on the fork and bread waits beside it
beats.summary: Some small studies suggest that eating vegetables and protein before carbohydrates lowers the blood sugar rise, but the evidence is early.

beats.scene: A person pushing a plate away after a huge lunch with a sleepy face
beats.summary: Hana learns to stop when she feels comfortably full, because a very large meal can make some people sleepy.

beats.scene: Hana eats her first steady plate and marks the afternoon in her diary
beats.summary: After her first steady lunch Hana scores her afternoon a six instead of her usual four, and Dev tells her to wait for more data.

beats.scene: A clock at seven, a bowl of cereal and a crossed-out slogan
beats.summary: People say that breakfast is the most important meal, but the evidence is mixed and the answer differs from person to person.

beats.scene: Hana on the bus holding a pastry and a paper cup
beats.summary: Hana's usual breakfast is a pastry on the bus, and she gets hungry again two hours later.

beats.scene: A bowl of porridge topped with nuts and a pot of tea
beats.summary: On the first day Hana tries porridge with nuts and finds that she stays full until lunch.

beats.scene: A plate with an empty place and a clock showing ten
beats.summary: On the second day she skips breakfast and feels hungry and short-tempered by half past ten.

beats.scene: Eggs on wholemeal toast with a sliced tomato beside a mug
beats.summary: On the third day Hana eats eggs on wholemeal toast, which she enjoys and finds filling.

beats.scene: A group of different people eating, skipping or snacking at a long table
beats.summary: Dev explains that some people feel fine without breakfast, and that children, pregnant women and people with diabetes should follow their own health advice.

beats.scene: A pan of oats on a stove with a sliced apple beside it
beats.summary: Oats are cheap and rich in fibre, and Hana soon makes them with fruit in the evening, ready for the morning.

beats.scene: A pot of plain yoghurt with berries and a spoon
beats.summary: Plain yoghurt with fruit is a quick breakfast, and it holds less sugar than sweetened pots.

beats.scene: Priya holds up a carton of juice and Dev shakes his head gently
beats.summary: Priya says that juice is healthy, and Dev says that it is a drink with sugar, while a whole fruit also brings fibre.

beats.scene: Hana ticks a breakfast on a chart that lists three options
beats.summary: Hana chooses porridge on busy days and eggs at weekends, because her diary shows that it suits her best.

beats.scene: Hana types with one hand and eats a sandwich over a keyboard
beats.summary: Hana usually eats lunch at her desk while she types, so she hardly notices what she has eaten.

beats.scene: Hana and Dev walk around a park in coats after eating lunch
beats.summary: A short walk after a meal lowers the rise in blood sugar in several small trials and may reduce sleepiness.

beats.scene: Two coats and a park path with a few orange leaves
beats.summary: They walk for fifteen minutes around the park, and Hana is warmer and more awake when she gets back.

beats.scene: A drawing of a leg muscle absorbing sugar from the blood
beats.summary: Active muscles take sugar from the blood, which may be why even a gentle walk after eating helps.

beats.scene: A plate on a table beside a closed laptop and a window
beats.summary: Dev suggests eating lunch away from the screen, because people eat more slowly and notice fullness better.

beats.scene: A small lunch box and a huge plate side by side
beats.summary: A huge, starchy lunch makes many people sleepy, and a moderate meal with protein and vegetables suits Hana better.

beats.scene: A staff canteen counter with a queue and a salad bar
beats.summary: In the canteen Hana learns to build a steady plate from what is on offer, with a salad, some beans and a bread roll.

beats.scene: Marcus and Hana walk down a corridor with a notebook and a coffee
beats.summary: Hana suggests a walking meeting, and Marcus, to everyone's surprise, tries it and enjoys it.

beats.scene: Rain on the office windows and two people climbing stairs
beats.summary: On a rainy day Hana and Dev walk up and down the stairs and along the corridor instead.

beats.scene: Hana puts a smiling face on her diary page for the third walking day
beats.summary: By the end of week two her diary shows that most of her walking days have higher afternoon scores than her sitting days.

beats.scene: Hana fills a water bottle at an office tap beside a colour chart
beats.summary: Even mild dehydration can lower focus and mood; thirst guides most healthy people, and drinks and food both supply water.

beats.scene: A drawing of a body outline filled mostly with blue
beats.summary: Water makes up a large part of the body, and every cell needs it for its work.

beats.scene: A hand holding a huge water bottle beside a warning sign
beats.summary: Dev says that thirst is a good guide for most healthy people, and that drinking vastly more than you need does not help.

beats.scene: A mug of tea and a cup of coffee beside a glass of water
beats.summary: Tea and coffee count towards your fluids, and the small diuretic effect of caffeine does not cancel them out.

beats.scene: A tall fizzy drink with sugar cubes stacked beside it in a cinema
beats.summary: Sugary drinks raise blood sugar quickly without making you feel full; water, tea and coffee without sugar are better.

beats.scene: A tall glass of orange juice beside a bowl of whole oranges
beats.summary: Juice and smoothies hold sugar without most of the fibre, so a small glass is fine, but a litre is a lot.

beats.scene: A can of diet drink beside a question mark on a laboratory bench
beats.summary: Diet drinks contain no sugar, and Dev says honestly that studies about their long-term effects are unclear.

beats.scene: A chart of seven pale to dark tones of yellow on a bathroom wall
beats.summary: Pale straw-coloured urine usually means enough water, and very dark urine is a sign to drink more.

beats.scene: Hana's desk with a bottle, a glass and a sticky note saying refill
beats.summary: Hana refills her bottle after every meeting, so that drinking becomes a habit and not a chore.

beats.scene: Hana tilts her head at a diary line about a clearer afternoon
beats.summary: Hana feels a little clearer on days when she drinks enough, but Dev says that she cannot prove it from a single week.

beats.scene: Hana opens a desk drawer holding a banana, nuts, yoghurt and an apple
beats.summary: Snacks that combine fibre and protein, such as fruit with nuts or yoghurt, keep energy steadier than sweets.

beats.scene: Priya and Hana stand in front of a glowing vending machine
beats.summary: At three o'clock Hana and Priya often walk to the vending machine and buy a bar of chocolate.

beats.scene: A hand reaches for a doughnut in a bakery window at midday
beats.summary: Sweet cravings are common and often follow poor sleep, stress or long gaps without eating; planning meals and snacks helps.

beats.scene: Hana looks at a glass of water and a timer showing ten minutes
beats.summary: When a craving comes, Hana waits ten minutes, drinks some water, and then decides what to eat without any blame.

beats.scene: A tin of biscuits with a lock crossed out beside a happy plate
beats.summary: Dev says that forbidding foods often backfires, so Hana keeps biscuits but eats them with her tea after lunch.

beats.scene: Hana stands in a kitchen holding a biscuit and a banana
beats.summary: Hana learns that tiredness can feel like hunger, so she asks herself when she last ate before she picks a snack.

beats.scene: A small handful of nuts in a palm beside a jar
beats.summary: A small handful of nuts is a good snack, although nuts are rich in energy, and people with nut allergies must avoid them.

beats.scene: An office fruit bowl with apples, bananas and a hand-written sign
beats.summary: Priya and Hana persuade Marcus to put a fruit bowl and a tub of nuts by the vending machine, and people begin to use it.

beats.scene: A weekly planner with a snack written on each afternoon
beats.summary: Hana plans her snacks each week, and she brings an apple with nut butter or yoghurt with fruit.

beats.scene: Hana writes two lines about snacks beside a drawing of a chocolate bar
beats.summary: Her diary shows that a planned snack at half past three leaves her steadier than a chocolate bar at three.

beats.scene: An open fridge with a takeaway menu and a lone lemon
beats.summary: Hana's fridge usually holds a takeaway menu and little else, and she often eats late and in a rush.

beats.scene: A calendar page for last spring with a crossed-out diet plan
beats.summary: Last spring Hana ate very little for a few weeks to lose weight, and she remembers being tired and cross.

beats.scene: A person at a table with a full bowl and a thoughtful frown
beats.summary: Dev says that the body needs enough food, and that anyone who wants to change their weight should ask a doctor or a dietitian.

beats.scene: A shopping list with oats, tinned beans, frozen peas, eggs and yoghurt
beats.summary: On Saturday Hana makes a short list of cheap, steady foods, with beans, frozen vegetables, oats, eggs and yoghurt.

beats.scene: Hana chops vegetables and fills boxes with rice and beans on Sunday
beats.summary: Cooking a big batch on the weekend makes steady meals easier on busy days.

beats.scene: A lunch box on a desk with lentil salad, bread and fruit
beats.summary: Hana's lunch: lentils or beans, vegetables, whole grains and fruit, which keep her energy steadier through the afternoon.

beats.scene: A grocery receipt beside a tin of lentils and a bag of frozen spinach
beats.summary: She is surprised to find that a week of steady lunches costs less than three takeaway meals.

beats.scene: A plate with a good ready meal and a bag of washed salad
beats.summary: Dev says that cooking is not a test, and that a good ready meal, a bag of salad and a tin of fish are fine too.

beats.scene: A table set for a late dinner with candles and a clock showing ten
beats.summary: Heavy meals late at night may disturb sleep for some people, so finish a large meal a few hours before bed if you can.

beats.scene: Hana sits with her diary and tea on Sunday evening
beats.summary: At the end of the cooking weekend Hana's diary shows steadier afternoons on most days, and she is cautiously proud.

beats.scene: Priya holds up a bottle of iron tablets in the office kitchen
beats.summary: Priya says that she takes iron tablets because she feels tired, and Hana wonders if she should buy some too.

beats.scene: Lentils, spinach, dried apricots and a small piece of meat on a board
beats.summary: Iron helps the blood to carry oxygen; beans, lentils, leafy greens, meat and fortified cereals contain it, and vitamin C helps absorption.

beats.scene: A drawing of a blood test tube with a doctor's hand
beats.summary: Low iron is a common cause of tiredness, but a blood test should find it, and iron pills should not be taken unless a doctor advises it.

beats.scene: A glass of fortified milk beside a drawing of a fish and an egg
beats.summary: Vitamin B12 comes from animal foods, so people who eat none are usually advised to take fortified foods or a supplement.

beats.scene: A sunny window and a small bottle of vitamin D drops
beats.summary: Sunlight helps the skin to make vitamin D, and in some countries health authorities advise a supplement in winter.

B1B2: Every afternoon at three o'clock, Hana's energy disappears and her eyes begin to close. She reaches for a strong coffee and a sweet biscuit, although she knows that they will not help for long.
At ten past three, the figures on Hana's spreadsheet seem to float across the screen. Her manager Marcus glances over from his desk and raises one eyebrow.
Her colleague Dev coaches a running club in the evenings, and he reads a lot about health. He offers to help Hana test what really gives steady energy, and what is only a story.
Dev takes a pen and writes three words on a note: proven, likely and unknown. He promises to give every claim one of these labels, so that Hana always knows how much to trust it.
Hana opens her desk drawer and shows Dev three boxes of special tea and a bottle of tablets. She has also tried a juice cleanse, and none of them has changed her afternoons.
They agree to run a four-week experiment, and they circle the dates on a calendar. Hana will change one habit at a time and watch what happens to her energy.
Hana buys a small notebook at lunchtime and draws three columns in it. Three times a day, at eleven, at three and at six, she will give her energy a score from one to ten.
Hana's first diary page shows a short night, three coffees and a skipped lunch. Her score at three is a sad two, and the page also has a brown coffee ring.
Dev gives her a gentle warning before they begin. One person's results are not proof for everyone, and tiredness that lasts for weeks should be checked by a doctor.

That evening Hana sits up in bed with her notebook and a lamp, and she feels hopeful for the first time in months. She decides to begin properly the next morning, with a glass of water and a short walk.
Dev draws a tiny cell on a notepad, with a lightning bolt in the middle. Every cell turns food and oxygen into usable energy, he says, and this is the heart of the whole subject.
Dev turns a biscuit packet over and points to the table of numbers on the back. Calories are simply a way of measuring the energy in food, he says, just as centimetres measure length.
Dev draws a heart, a pair of lungs and a thermometer. Most of the body's energy is spent on simply staying alive, he says, by keeping the heart beating, the lungs working and the body warm.
Dev points to the top of his head and says that the brain is small but hungry. It uses about a fifth of the body's energy, so thinking hard really does cost fuel.
Dev draws a tired face with three question marks above it. Feeling tired is a signal, he says, and it can come from sleep, mood, food, health and stress, not only from a lack of calories.
Hana takes a slow deep breath beside the open window. Dev reminds her that oxygen matters as much as food, because the blood carries it from the lungs to every cell in the body.

Dev draws three faces and labels them sleepy, body-tired and mind-tired. Each kind needs a different remedy, he says, because a nap will not rest a tired mind and a coffee will not rest tired muscles.
Dev explains that the body does not work like a car with a tiny fuel tank. It stores energy in the liver, in the muscles and as fat, and it can draw on these stores between meals.
Hana asks Dev whether the answer is simply to eat more calories each day. He says that it is not so simple, because eating too little and eating too much can both leave a person feeling flat.
Priya, who sits at the next desk, peers over the screen and spots the diary. She says that she lives on energy drinks, so Dev adds them to his list of things to examine.
Dev points to the big clock on the office wall and says that the body has one too. It runs for about twenty-four hours, he explains, and makes us more alert at some times and sleepier at others.
A master clock in the brain keeps time for many smaller clocks in other parts of the body. They work best when they all agree, Dev says, a little like musicians following one conductor.
Dev draws a wavy line across the notepad and marks the hours. Alertness rises through the morning, peaks near midday and dips in the early afternoon, in a gentle wave that repeats every single day.
In some studies, volunteers were kept from eating and yet they still felt the early afternoon dip. This suggests that lunch cannot be the only cause, although a big meal can make the dip feel worse.
Dev, who is wide awake at dawn, tells Hana that people differ in their natural timing. Some are larks who wake early, some are owls who stay up late, and genes play a part in which one you are.
Hana looks at the calendar and notices that Marcus's Tuesday team meeting begins at three fifteen. That is exactly the hour of her deepest dip, and it is a poor time to think hard.
Hana writes her hardest tasks in a morning column and her simple tasks in an afternoon column. She keeps long reports for late morning, when she is sharpest, and answers easy emails at three.

Priya's brother is a nurse who works night shifts and goes home as others arrive at work. Working against the clock is truly hard on energy, Dev says, so shift workers deserve extra patience and extra care.
Dev says that a steady routine helps the clock, and he asks Hana to keep her times regular. Sleeping very late at the weekend can push the clock out of step, which people call social jet lag.
On the third day Hana still feels the afternoon dip, but she writes a new note in her diary. It is a wave from her clock, she decides, and it is not a fault in her.
Dev says that light is the strongest signal that tells the body clock the day has begun. It reaches the brain through the eyes, even when a person is not looking at anything in particular.
Hana starts getting off the bus one stop early, near a small park. She walks the last ten minutes in the morning light, and she feels a little silly and a little proud.
Dev says that even on a cloudy day the light outdoors is far stronger than the light in a typical office. Our eyes adjust so well that we hardly notice how dim indoor light really is.
Hana asks Marcus if she can move her desk beside the window, and he agrees with a shrug and a smile. She pulls up the blind and feels the daylight on her face.
Dev says that morning light helps to set the body clock, and that this is well supported. How much it improves one person's energy is less certain, so he labels that part likely and not proven.
Hana now opens her bedroom curtains the minute her alarm rings. The room floods with light, and she finds it a little easier to leave her bed.
In the dark months it is harder to get light, so a lunchtime walk matters more. Dev adds that anyone who feels very low every winter should talk to a doctor, who can advise on bright-light lamps.
Dev reminds Hana never to look straight at the sun, because it can damage the eyes. On strong days she should also protect her skin with a hat or sunscreen.
After four days of morning walks, Hana's diary shows higher scores before lunch on the bright days. Her afternoons, however, have hardly changed, and she writes this down honestly.
Dev gives a thumbs up beside her diary in the sunlit office kitchen. A mixed result is still a result, he says, because the experiment is working when it shows what does not help.
Dev says that adults are usually advised to sleep for at least seven hours a night. Sleep is the base of daytime energy, he adds, and nothing else on their list can replace it.
Hana counts the hours between her bedtime and her alarm, and she is shocked. She goes to bed after midnight and wakes at half past six, so she sleeps for about six hours on most nights.
After a short night people tend to feel hungrier and to crave sweet and salty food. Poor sleep can therefore look like a food problem, when the real trouble began the night before.
Dev draws a wave with steps that go down and up. Sleep moves through light and deep stages in cycles of about an hour and a half, and each stage seems to do different work.
Hana asks whether a long lie-in at the weekend can repay a week of short nights. Dev says that it repays only part of the debt, and that the evidence about catching up on sleep is mixed.
Hana sets a reminder on her phone for half past ten each night. She decides to treat bedtime like an appointment that she cannot cancel, even when a film is almost over.

On Saturday morning Hana wakes at the same time as on a work day, and she feels grumpy all through breakfast. By Sunday, however, she feels a little more normal, and the clock seems to be catching up.
Dev says that loud snoring with gasps, or feeling tired after a full night in bed, could be a sleep disorder. Anyone who notices these signs should talk to a doctor, because they are treatable.
If Hana lies awake for a long time, she gets up and does something quiet, such as reading, until she feels sleepy. Trouble sleeping that lasts for weeks is a good reason to see a doctor.
At the end of the first week, after a few nights of seven hours, Hana's dip at three is smaller. It has not gone, and Dev warns her not to oversell the result.

Hana, who has hidden under a blanket every morning of her adult life, feels strangely excused.

Hana looks at the shared calendar and notices that Marcus's Tuesday team meeting begins at three fifteen, which is precisely the hour of her deepest dip. It is a hard time to think clearly, let alone to say something clever, and she has been nodding silently in that meeting for two years. She resolves to bring it up at a better moment, with evidence in her hand.

Hana divides her page into two columns and puts her hardest tasks in the morning one and her simple tasks in the afternoon one. She now keeps long reports for late morning, when most people are at their sharpest, and she saves routine emails and filing for the dip at three. The change costs nothing, and it feels like having a quiet word with her own body.

Priya mentions that her brother is a nurse who works night shifts and walks home at dawn just as other people are arriving at work. Dev says that forcing the body to be awake when its clock says night is truly hard on energy, and that shift workers deserve extra patience and extra advice from their doctors. Hana looks at her own small problem and feels the first stirrings of perspective.

Dev says that a steady routine helps the clock to keep good time, and he asks Hana to keep her bedtime and her waking time fairly regular. Sleeping very late at the weekend can push the clock out of step with the working week, an effect that people call social jet lag, even though nobody has left the country. Hana makes a careful note in her diary and tries very hard not to look guilty about last Sunday.

On the third day Hana still feels the afternoon dip as keenly as ever, but she writes a new kind of note in her diary. It is a wave from her body clock, she decides, and it is not a fault in her character or a sign of some hidden illness. Knowing the reason does not remove the wave, yet it takes away most of the shame.

Dev says that light is the strongest signal that tells the body clock that the day has begun. It reaches the brain through the eyes, even when a person is not looking at anything in particular, and the brain uses it to keep the whole orchestra in time. A dim bedroom and a dim office, he adds, give that conductor very little to work with.

Hana begins getting off the bus one stop early, beside a small park with a row of chestnut trees. She walks the last ten minutes of her journey in the morning light, feeling a little silly at first and then a little proud, as the sky turns from grey to pale gold. By the time she reaches her desk, she is already more awake than usual.

Dev says that even on a grey and cloudy day the light outdoors is far stronger than the light in a typical office. Our eyes adjust so well that we hardly notice how dim an indoor room is, which is why a short walk can feel like switching on a lamp. Hana looks up at the pale ceiling lights above her desk and, for the first time, sees them as rather weak.

Hana asks Marcus whether she can move her desk beside the window, and he agrees with a shrug and a smile, since nobody else wanted that corner. She pulls up the blind and feels the daylight settle on her face, and for the first time in months she can see the clouds moving over the car park. It is not a perfect view, but it is a real one, and she decides that it will do very well.

Dev says that it is well established that morning light helps to set the body clock, and he labels that part of the story proven. Hana now pulls back her bedroom curtains the very minute that her alarm rings, before she can negotiate with herself. It is a small act, but it seems to tell her body that the day has genuinely started.

Dev reminds her that in the dark months it is harder to find morning light, so a lunchtime walk matters even more than it does in summer. He adds that anyone who feels very low every winter should talk to a doctor, who can advise on options such as bright-light lamps and other help. Hana, who lives in a country of long grey winters, is glad to know that she is not simply being dramatic.

Dev reminds Hana never to look straight at the sun, because the glare can damage the eyes, and he explains that morning light does not need such risks. When the sun is strong she should also protect her skin with a hat, shade or sunscreen, since the aim is to feel better and not to turn into a tomato. Hana packs a wide hat into her bag the next morning and feels like an extremely sensible person.

After four days of morning walks, Hana studies her diary and sees that her scores before lunch are higher on the bright days. Her afternoons, however, have barely changed, and she writes that down with equal honesty, because Dev has taught her that a result which spoils the story is still a result. She feels a little disappointed and a little scientific at the same time, which is a surprisingly pleasant mixture.

Dev gives a thumbs up as they stand together in the sunlit office kitchen, holding two cups of tea and a banana each. A mixed result is still a result, he tells her, because an experiment is working when it shows what does not help as clearly as what does. Hana says that she is starting to like being wrong, as long as it is useful.

Dev says that adults are usually advised to sleep for at least seven hours each night, and that some people need a little more. Hana, who has been building a tower on a very small foundation, listens with sinking recognition.

Hana counts the hours between her real bedtime and her alarm, and she is quietly shocked by the answer. She scrolls her phone until after midnight and wakes at half past six, so she is sleeping for about six hours on most nights, and for less than that on bad ones. She had always told herself that she was one of those people who did not need much.

Dev explains that after a short night people tend to feel hungrier and to crave sweet and salty food, and that this is a well-studied effect. Poor sleep can therefore look like a food problem, when the real trouble began hours earlier, in the bedroom and not in the kitchen. Hana thinks of every biscuit that she has ever eaten at three o'clock, and she blushes.

Dev draws a wave with steps that go down and then up, and he explains that sleep moves through light and deep stages in cycles of about an hour and a half. Each stage seems to do different work, with deep sleep important for the body and dreaming sleep for the mind, although scientists are still learning how it all fits together. Hana says that, judging by the way she has felt lately, she has not done much of the deep kind.

Hana asks whether a long lie-in at the weekend can repay a whole week of short nights. Dev says that it seems to repay only part of the debt, that the evidence about catching up on sleep is mixed, and that regular sleep every night is a safer plan than a big payment on Sunday. Hana, who has been living on sleep credit for years and has never once looked at the bill, nods slowly.

Hana sets a gentle reminder on her phone for half past ten each night, with a title that says go to bed, you clever person. She decides to treat bedtime like an appointment that she cannot cancel, even when a film is almost over or a message demands an answer. The first night she complains, the second night she sighs, and the third night she hardly notices.

On Saturday morning Hana drags herself up at the same time as on a work day, and she is grumpy all through breakfast. By Sunday, however, the grumpiness has faded, and she realises that her body clock seems to be settling into a rhythm that it has never been given before. She spends the sunlit afternoon in the park and feels, rather to her surprise, quite cheerful.

Dev says that loud snoring with gasps or pauses in breathing, or feeling very tired after a full night in bed, could be a sign of a sleep disorder. Anyone who notices these signs should talk to a doctor, he stresses, because such problems are treatable and no amount of green tea will cure them. Hana says that she will mention it to her sister, who snores like a motorbike.

When Hana lies awake for a long time, she follows Dev's advice, which is to get up and do something quiet in dim light until sleepiness returns. Watching the clock and worrying about sleep usually makes it worse, he says, and trouble sleeping that lasts for weeks is a good reason to see a doctor. Hana puts a battered paperback beside her bed and, for once in her life, feels properly prepared for the night.

At the end of the first week, after several nights of seven hours, Hana notices that her dip at three is smaller and shorter than before. It has not gone away, and Dev warns her gently that a week of data is not proof and that she must not oversell the result to herself or anyone else. She writes a very small note of thanks in her diary, and the sight of it makes both of them laugh.

Hana looks through her coffee-shop receipts and admits that she drinks three coffees and a fizzy cola on every working day. Dev does not judge her for it, and he asks only what she believes the coffee does for her, since a habit is easier to change once it has been understood. She says that it wakes her up, and he says that it is time to look more closely.

Dev explains that a chemical called adenosine builds up in the brain through the day and gradually makes people feel sleepy. Caffeine blocks the receptors that detect it, so the sleepiness is still there, but the brain cannot feel it for a while, rather as if somebody had muffled the alarm. Hana looks down at her cup with a new respect, and also with a trace of resentment at being fooled for so long.

Dev says that caffeine does not create energy at all, but hides tiredness for a while by blocking the message. When the drug wears off, the sleepiness is still waiting, and sometimes it feels worse than before, which may explain why Hana reaches for another cup at three. Hana calls this a bank loan with a terrible interest rate, and Dev admits that the comparison is better than any of his own.

Dev draws a coffee cup with a long fading tail of hours, and he explains that caffeine leaves the body slowly. In the average adult about half is still present after about five hours, although the figure varies a great deal from one person to another, and some people feel an afternoon cup well into the night. Hana looks at her four o'clock cup with real suspicion and wonders how many sleepless nights it has quietly caused.

Hana moves all her coffee to the morning and stops drinking it after lunch, in order to protect her sleep. At the tea kiosk downstairs she waves politely away the cup that she would normally buy at three, and she buys a peppermint tea in its place, feeling as if she has won a tiny war. Her hand, however, trembles slightly in protest, and she holds the cup of peppermint tea a little too tightly.

Dev tells her that for most adults up to about four cups of coffee a day is considered safe, so her habit was not outrageous, only badly timed. Pregnant people are advised to have less, though, and should ask their doctor or midwife how much is right for them, and the same goes for anyone with a heart condition. Hana is relieved to hear that she is not a criminal after all, and that her problem was timing and not quantity.

When Hana cuts her coffee down suddenly, she gets a thudding headache and feels sluggish and cross for two long days. Dev says that this is common after stopping caffeine, that it usually passes within a few days, and that cutting down gradually is kinder than stopping all at once. She admits that this advice would have been far more useful on Monday morning, before the headache had made her so rude.

Dev reminds her that tea, cola and dark chocolate also contain caffeine, and that even decaffeinated coffee is not entirely free of it. A cup of strong tea at seven in the evening, he points out, is not nearly as innocent as it looks, and neither is a square of dark chocolate before bed. Hana quietly moves her chocolate to the morning drawer of her desk and feels slightly as if she has been caught.

Some people feel jittery or anxious after caffeine, and some notice a pounding or racing heart, which is a reason to take it seriously. Dev says that anyone who is worried about these effects, or about their heartbeat, should ask a doctor and should not simply push through it for the sake of a diary. Hana says that she feels fine, only sleepy, and Dev nods, satisfied, but he asks her to tell him at once if that ever changes.

After four days of morning-only coffee, Hana circles two entries in her diary with a flourish. She is sleeping better and her afternoons are slightly steadier, although she misses the pleasant ritual of her three o'clock cup and says so out loud, to nobody in particular. Dev replies that a ritual can be kept with a different drink, and he fills her mug with hot water and a lemon slice.

Dev draws a slice of bread that turns, step by step, into a pile of small sugar cubes. Carbohydrates in food are broken down in the gut into glucose, which is the sugar that travels in the blood, and which the body uses as one of its main fuels. Hana says that it feels odd to learn that her toast is quietly becoming sugar inside her.

Dev adds a small brain to his drawing and says that glucose is the body's main quick fuel, on which the brain depends heavily. A steady supply therefore matters far more than a sudden flood, he explains, especially for a mind that must stay clear through a long afternoon of spreadsheets and meetings. Hana writes steady, not sudden on a sticky note and sticks it to her mug.

Dev draws a tiny key opening the door of a cell, and he explains that this is how insulin works, as far as a simple drawing can show. This hormone, made in the pancreas, helps to move glucose from the blood into the cells, where it can be used or stored for later. Hana says that it is a clever system and that she hopes her keys never go missing.

Dev draws a gentle wave on his graph and explains that blood sugar rises after every meal in every healthy person and then falls again. This rise and fall is normal, he stresses, and it is the body doing its job, so nobody should be frightened of a wave as long as the wave is not too high or too steep. Hana relaxes a little at that word, normal, and she asks whether she may write it on her wall in large letters.

Dev explains that foods that are digested quickly, such as sugary drinks and white bread, raise blood sugar faster than foods rich in fibre. Lentils, for example, release their sugar slowly over a long time, and so they produce a gentle hill in place of a sharp mountain. Hana, who has never thought of lentils as exciting, gives them a respectful glance.

Dev shows her a chart called the glycaemic index, which ranks foods by how quickly they raise blood sugar compared with pure glucose. It is only a rough guide, he warns, because cooking, ripeness and the foods eaten alongside it all change the result, and nobody eats a food entirely alone. Hana says that a rough guide is better than no guide, and he agrees.

Dev tells her that fibre, protein and fat all slow down digestion, and that the three of them work like a gentle brake on the stomach. A balanced meal therefore raises blood sugar more gently than a plate of plain white pasta, and it often leaves a person feeling fuller for longer afterwards. Hana makes a mental note to add a handful of vegetables to every pasta night.

Hana tests plain white toast on one morning and toast with an egg on the next, and she records how she feels at eleven. She is fuller and calmer after the egg, but Dev reminds her that a single test on a single person proves very little, because many other things change from one day to another. He still labels the idea likely rather than proven, and Hana is pleased to have a small piece of evidence that is her own.

Dev says that a large swing in blood sugar may make some people feel tired and shaky a few hours after a sugary snack. The evidence, however, is mixed, and the afternoon dip is known to happen even without such a swing, so a sugar crash cannot be the whole explanation for what Hana feels. She finds it oddly comforting that the picture is complicated, since it means that nobody has been fooled by a single simple trick.

Dev explains that the healthy body keeps blood sugar within a narrow range, rather like a thermostat that keeps a house at one temperature. In diabetes, that control does not work as it should, either because the body makes too little insulin or because the cells do not respond to it well, which is why the condition needs a doctor's care. Hana listens quietly and, for once, does not make a joke, because she is thinking about people she knows who live with it.

Whole grains and beans digest slowly and keep their natural fibre, which makes them far better for steady energy than refined grains. Dev lines up a loaf of wholemeal bread, a jar of oats and a tin of beans on the kitchen counter like a small team of reliable athletes. Hana looks at them with more interest than she has ever shown a loaf of bread.

Dev draws a grain of wheat and divides it into layers, with a label for each one. A whole grain keeps its fibre-rich outer layer and its germ, whereas white flour has lost most of them in the mill, and with them has gone much of the fibre and some of the vitamins. Hana asks whether white bread is therefore forbidden, and he laughs and says that nothing is.

Dev holds up a tin of beans, a bag of lentils and a pot of chickpeas as if he were presenting prizes. These foods give fibre, protein and iron at a very low price, he says, and they are the unsung heroes of the steady plate, which cost far less than a coffee and keep better than almost anything else. Hana admits that she has never bought a lentil on purpose in her whole life, and that she is not entirely sure how to start.

Vegetables should fill about half the plate, Dev says, and the colours of the rainbow make a good rough rule. Frozen and tinned vegetables count just as much as fresh ones, and they are often cheaper, quicker to prepare and less likely to turn into a sad soup at the bottom of the fridge. Hana opens her freezer at home that evening, finds nothing but ice and a lonely pizza box, and decides to go shopping on Saturday.

Protein comes from eggs, fish, yoghurt, tofu, beans, nuts and meat, and there are plenty of choices for every taste and budget. It slows digestion and helps people to feel full, so a modest portion at each meal is a sound habit, although nobody needs to pile the plate high. Hana is relieved to find that her favourite scrambled eggs count as part of the plan.

Healthy fats, such as those in nuts, olive oil and avocado, are not the enemy, Dev says, and the old fear of all fat was far too crude. They slow digestion and make many foods taste better, which helps a person to enjoy a meal and to feel satisfied when it is over. Hana, who has avoided every bit of fat for years and has tasted nothing but sadness, looks suddenly cheerful at the thought of olive oil.

Dev draws a plate in three parts and fills each one in with coloured pens. About half is vegetables and fruit, about a quarter is whole grains or other starchy foods, and about a quarter is protein, with a little healthy fat on the side. None of it needs to be perfect or measured, and Hana pins the drawing above her desk, where it watches over her like a small and kindly inspector.

Some small studies suggest that eating vegetables and protein before the carbohydrates in a meal lowers the rise in blood sugar afterwards. Dev calls the evidence early and the studies small, and he labels the idea unknown, adding that Hana may try it if it is easy and enjoyable but should not worry if it is not. She decides that she will try it whenever a salad arrives first at a restaurant, and that she will forget it the rest of the time.

Hana learns to stop eating when she feels comfortably full and not stuffed, a skill that she suspects she lost somewhere in her teens. A very large meal can leave some people sleepy and slow, he says, while a moderate one is usually easier for the body to handle, although people differ and hunger is not a flaw. She slows down and notices the taste of her food for the first time in months.

After her first steady lunch of beans, vegetables and wholemeal bread, Hana scores her afternoon a six instead of her usual four. Dev tells her to be pleased but to wait for more data before she believes it, since one good day might be luck, a sunny sky or a surprisingly short meeting. Hana says that she will enjoy the six anyway and hold the explanation lightly.

Many people say that breakfast is the most important meal of the day, and the slogan has been printed on cereal boxes for generations. Dev says that the evidence is mixed and that the answer seems to differ from one person to another, so he labels the slogan unknown and not proven. Hana, who has believed it all her life, finds it strange to hold such a famous idea up to the light.

Hana's usual breakfast is a flaky pastry eaten on the bus, with a coffee that she carries carefully round every corner. She feels hungry again two hours later, and that is the moment when the office biscuit tin begins to look like a trusted friend. Dev says that her body is not being greedy, but simply asking for the meal that it did not receive.

On the first day of the test, Hana eats a warm bowl of porridge with a handful of chopped nuts and a spoonful of seeds. She stays comfortably full until lunch, and she does not once think about the biscuit tin, which sits in the corner of the office looking rather neglected. She writes a seven in her diary and draws a small bowl beside it.

On the second day of the test she skips breakfast on purpose, to see what happens. By half past ten she feels hungry, short-tempered and distracted, and she snaps at a printer that has done nothing worse than jam, which is entirely in its nature. She records a four in her diary and a note that apologises to the printer.

On the third day Hana eats soft eggs on wholemeal toast with a sliced tomato and a little pepper. She enjoys every mouthful, finds the meal pleasantly filling, and decides that it feels like a proper beginning to the day, which she has not felt since she was a student. She writes a seven in her diary and adds a small and happy egg.

Dev explains that some people feel perfectly fine without breakfast, and that skipping it may even suit them if they eat well later in the day. Children, pregnant women and people with diabetes, however, should follow their own health advice and not copy what works for other people, because their needs are different. Hana concludes that the soundest rule is the one that suits the individual, and that any universal prescription about breakfast deserves a certain suspicion.

Oats are cheap, rich in fibre and wonderfully flexible, and they can be cooked with milk or water in a few minutes on the stove. She finds that she looks forward to it even on the greyest of mornings.

Plain yoghurt with fruit makes a quick breakfast that needs no cooking and no washing up, apart from a spoon. Dev gives it a firm thumbs up and calls it practical, affordable and almost impossible to get wrong on a rushed morning.

Priya holds up a carton of orange juice at the office kitchen table and declares that it is a perfectly healthy breakfast. Dev says gently that it is a drink with a good deal of sugar in it, whereas a whole piece of fruit also brings fibre and takes longer to eat, so it fills a person up more. Priya says that she will think about it, which is her polite way of saying no.

Hana looks at her chart and chooses porridge on busy weekdays and eggs at the weekend, because those are the two breakfasts that her diary favours. She is quietly proud to have decided with evidence and not with a slogan, and she notices that nobody has told her what she ought to want. Dev says that this is the whole point of an experiment, and that it works only for her.

Hana usually eats her lunch at her desk with one hand on the keyboard and her eyes on the screen.
