Dev watches her chew with great sympathy, and he gently remarks that food eaten in a hurry is rarely remembered by anybody.

Dev tells Hana that in several small trials a short walk after a meal lowered the rise in blood sugar that normally follows it. It may also reduce sleepiness in the afternoon, although the studies are small and the effects differ from person to person, and he labels it likely and not proven. He then invites her to test it with him on Monday, and she cannot think of a good excuse.

They put on their coats and walk for fifteen minutes around the park, where a few orange leaves are still clinging to the trees. When they return, Hana is warmer, more awake and slightly out of breath, and she has the feeling that someone has opened a window in her head. She was sure that she would hate it, and she is annoyed to find that she does not.

Dev draws a leg muscle and shows an arrow of sugar flowing into it from the blood. Active muscles use glucose for fuel, he explains, and they can take it up even when insulin is scarce, which may be why even a gentle walk after eating seems to help. Hana likes the idea that a walk is like paying a small bill that the body would otherwise leave outstanding.

Dev suggests that Hana should eat her lunch in the break room, away from the screen and the inbox. People tend to eat more slowly when they are not distracted, he explains, and they notice more easily when they are full, although the research on mindful eating is modest and he labels it unknown. Hana tries it anyway because the break room has a window and a plant.

A huge lunch heavy with starch makes many people sleepy, and she can feel it in her own heavy eyelids. A moderate meal with protein and vegetables suits Hana far better, and on those days she feels clear and calm for much longer, with no need to hide under the desk. Dev points out that bodies differ, but that her diary seems to agree with the theory.

In the staff canteen Hana learns to build a steady plate from whatever happens to be on offer that day. She chooses a salad, a scoop of beans, a piece of chicken and a bread roll, and she leaves the chips alone without feeling that she has made any dreadful sacrifice. Dev says that she may have the chips on another day, because eating well is a pattern and not a performance.

Hana suggests a walking meeting, and Marcus, to everyone's surprise, agrees to try it on Thursday. They walk the length of the corridor and back with a notebook between them and a coffee in his hand, and they agree on the project plan in half the usual time. Marcus says that he is not sure whether it was the walking or the lack of chairs.

On a rainy day Hana and Dev decide against the park and walk up and down the stairs and along the corridor instead. It is not as pretty as the park, and the carpet is the colour of porridge, but it still gets them moving and gets them away from the screens for a quarter of an hour. Hana decides that the weather is a poor excuse and an even poorer enemy, and she vows never to blame the rain again.

By the end of week two, Hana's diary shows that most of her walking days have higher afternoon scores than her sitting days. She draws a smiling face beside the third walking day and shows it proudly to Dev, who tells her that the pattern is encouraging but that it does not yet prove cause and effect. She says that she will happily take encouraging for now, and he laughs and adds that she is turning into a proper scientist.

Hana fills a large water bottle at the office tap, beside a small chart that shows shades of yellow. Even mild dehydration can lower concentration and mood, Dev tells her, although thirst is a remarkably reliable guide for most healthy people, and drinks and food both supply water. She decides to sip regularly and to treat her thirst as a signal worth hearing.

Water makes up a large part of the human body, and every cell needs it in order to do its work. Dev draws a body outline and shades most of it blue, which makes Hana feel like a walking bottle, and he explains that we lose water all day through breathing, sweating and the toilet. It must therefore be replaced, but the body is skilful at asking for it.

Dev says that thirst is a good guide for most healthy people, and that the old rule about eight glasses was never carved in stone. Drinking vastly more than you need will not give you extra energy, and in rare cases it can even cause harm, so the sensible aim is to drink when thirsty and to notice the colour of your urine. Hana puts down her enormous bottle, picks up a smaller one, and decides to trust her thirst a little more.

Dev says that tea and coffee count towards a person's daily fluids, which comes as a great relief to Hana's pride. The mild diuretic effect of caffeine, he explains, does not cancel out the water in the cup, especially for people who drink it regularly, although a lot of caffeine late in the day can still disturb sleep. She raises her mug of peppermint tea in a cheerful salute, and Dev solemnly clinks his own mug against it.

A tall cup of fizzy drink with several spoonfuls of sugar in it raises blood sugar quickly without making a person feel properly full. Water, tea and coffee without sugar are better choices for most of the day, Dev says, although a sweet drink now and then at a party is not a disaster. Hana remembers the large cinema drink that she used to carry like a trophy.

Juice and smoothies contain a good deal of sugar and have lost much of the fibre that whole fruit provides. A small glass is perfectly fine, Dev says, but a large carton drunk in one sitting is a significant amount of sugar that will not fill anyone up. Hana looks at the whole oranges in the fruit bowl and decides that she will eat one.

Diet drinks contain no sugar, and for many people they make a useful swap from sugary ones. Dev says honestly that studies on their long-term effects are unclear and sometimes contradict each other, so he labels the question unknown and refuses to pretend to know more than he does. Hana says that this is the most trustworthy thing a health person has ever told her.

There is a chart of seven yellow shades pinned inside the office bathroom, which Hana finds funny and useful in equal measure. Pale, straw-coloured urine usually means that a person has enough water, whereas very dark urine is a sign that they should drink more, unless some medicine or food has coloured it. Dev adds that unusual colours that last for days, or come with pain, should always be checked by a doctor.

Hana sticks a small note on her bottle that says refill, and she fills it again after every meeting. In that way, drinking becomes a habit attached to something she already does, and not a chore that depends on her memory or her willpower. Dev says that this trick works for many habits, and that psychologists like to call it stacking.

Hana feels a little clearer on the days when she drinks enough, and she records it in her diary with a small drawing of a drop. Dev says that she cannot prove it from a single week of notes, because many things change at once, but that it is a fair thing to keep watching. She underlines the word watching and decides that it sums up the whole experiment.

Hana opens her desk drawer and proudly presents a banana, a bag of nuts, a pot of yoghurt and a bruised apple. Snacks that combine fibre and protein, such as fruit with nuts or yoghurt, keep energy steadier than sweets do, Dev explains, because the sugar arrives more slowly and the stomach feels satisfied for longer. Hana says that the drawer looks like a very small and very polite shop, and Dev agrees that it is open all day.

At three o'clock Hana and Priya have long walked together to the glowing vending machine in the corridor, like two pilgrims. They buy a bar of chocolate and a packet of crisps, and they call it a reward for surviving another dull afternoon, although both of them are usually more tired an hour later. Dev points out that the ritual is lovely, even if the snack is not.

Sweet cravings are common and perfectly human, and they often follow poor sleep, stress, boredom or long gaps without a meal. Planning meals and snacks helps a great deal, Dev says, and so does treating oneself with kindness and not with punishment, since guilt rarely makes anyone stronger. Hana stares at the doughnuts in the bakery window on her way to work and sighs a long and honest sigh.

When a craving comes, Hana sets a timer for ten minutes and drinks a glass of water while she waits. When the timer rings, she decides what to eat, without any blame whichever way she chooses, and sometimes the craving has faded and sometimes it has not. She notes that the pause itself gives her a feeling of being in charge.

Dev says that forbidding a food often backfires, since the very thing that is banned tends to become more tempting, and that the evidence for strict bans is weak. Hana therefore keeps her biscuits, but she eats them with her tea after lunch and not as an emergency rescue at three o'clock, and she enjoys them more than before. Dev says that this is an excellent example of a sensible compromise, and that most lasting habits are built in exactly this way.

Hana learns that feeling tired can feel very much like feeling hungry, and that the two signals often arrive together and in disguise. She now asks herself when she last ate before choosing a snack, and she discovers that a short walk and a glass of water sometimes help more than a biscuit does. If her last meal was long ago, however, she eats, and she feels no shame.

A small handful of nuts makes a good snack, since they bring protein, fibre and healthy fat in one convenient package. They are rich in energy, however, so a handful is plenty, and people with a nut allergy must avoid them completely, as one of Hana's colleagues unfortunately knows only too well. She decides to keep a separate pot of seeds in the drawer for him to share.

Priya and Hana persuade Marcus to put a fruit bowl and a tub of mixed seeds beside the vending machine, and he agrees after a short and rather embarrassed silence. Within a week, people begin to take the apples and the bananas, and the vending machine looks a little lonelier, although it still has a few faithful customers. Marcus claims the idea as his own at the next staff meeting, and nobody minds in the least, least of all Hana.

Hana now plans her snacks at the start of each week and writes them in a small planner on her desk. She brings an apple with nut butter on Monday, yoghurt with fruit on Tuesday and a handful of nuts on Wednesday, and she feels pleasantly like a person who runs her own life. Dev says that a plan made on a calm Sunday is wiser than a decision made at three.

Hana's diary shows that a planned snack at half past three leaves her steadier than a chocolate bar eaten at three, and she writes two cheerful lines about it beside a small drawing of the bar. Dev says that the result fits what he expected from the science, but that she should keep watching, since the diary is the only authority that she can truly trust. Hana says that she still likes chocolate, and he says that so does he.

Hana's fridge usually holds a takeaway menu, half a lemon and a jar of mustard that has outlived two flats. She often eats late and in a rush, standing up, which is not a good plan for steady energy, as Dev points out with great tact. Hana says that her fridge is minimalist, and he says that it is also nearly empty.

Last spring Hana ate very little for several weeks, because she wanted to lose weight in time for a wedding. She remembers being tired, cold and cross all day, and she lost her patience with everyone, including a very kind waiter who had done nothing wrong. Dev nods and says that very strict dieting can drain energy, which is exactly what she experienced.

Dev says gently that the body needs enough food in order to work well, and that eating too little is one of the surest ways to feel flat. Anyone who wants to change their weight should ask a doctor or a registered dietitian for advice that fits their own life, he adds, because that is a separate subject from their experiment. Hana is glad that nobody is telling her what she ought to weigh, and she says that she feels more relaxed already.

On Saturday morning Hana writes a short shopping list that includes oats, tinned beans, frozen vegetables, eggs and plain yoghurt. It is the first proper list that she has made in months, and she feels almost alarmingly grown up as she walks through the supermarket with a basket and a purpose. She walks past the biscuit aisle with her chin held high and finds, to her great surprise, that she hardly misses it at all.

On Sunday afternoon Hana chops a mountain of vegetables, simmers a big pot of lentils and cooks a large pan of brown rice. Cooking a big batch at the weekend makes steady meals far easier on the busy days to come, and it fills her flat with a warm and friendly smell. She divides the food into neat boxes for the week ahead and feels like a very well-organised and rather smug squirrel.

Hana's lunch box holds a lentil salad with chopped vegetables, a thick slice of wholemeal bread and a piece of fruit. These foods, rich in fibre and protein, keep her energy steadier through the long afternoon, and they cost only a fraction of what she used to spend on sandwiches. She eats it at the break room table and she looks forward to it.

Hana is surprised to find that a whole week of steady lunches costs less than three of her usual takeaway meals. Beans, lentils and frozen vegetables are cheap, they keep for a long time, and they are not at all as dull as she had feared when she began, she tells Dev. He says that she may now call herself a thrifty person with a healthy bank account.

Dev says firmly that cooking is not a test of character, and that nobody should feel guilty about a ready meal now and then. A good ready meal, a bag of washed salad and a tin of fish make a perfectly decent dinner, especially on an evening when a person is very tired and has nothing left to give. Hana says that this is the kindest thing a health expert has said to her.

Dev says that heavy meals late at night may disturb sleep for some people, so it is sensible to finish a large meal a few hours before bed if you can. Hana tries it on Wednesday, when she eats dinner at seven instead of ten, and she wakes up the next morning feeling lighter and more rested than she has for a long time. She notes in her diary that this is only one data point and not a law of nature, and Dev approves of the careful wording.

On Sunday evening, at the end of her cooking weekend, Hana sits with her diary and a mug of tea and reads the last fortnight with care. It shows steadier afternoons on most days, with a few ordinary bumps, and she feels cautiously proud of a change that she did not believe was possible. Dev tells her to keep the pride and the caution, since they make a good pair.

In the office kitchen, Priya holds up a bottle of iron tablets that she bought from a website, and she explains that she takes them whenever she feels tired. She suggests that Hana might want to buy a bottle too, and Hana, who has bought several miracles in her time, feels an old temptation stir. Dev asks them both to wait a moment and to hear what the evidence says before they hand over any more of their money.

Dev explains that iron helps the blood to carry oxygen around the body, which is why a lack of it can leave a person pale, breathless and tired. Beans, lentils, leafy greens, meat and fortified cereals contain iron, and vitamin C from fruit or vegetables helps the body to absorb the iron that comes from plants. Hana looks at her lunch box that afternoon and silently congratulates the lentils on being a thoroughly respectable source of iron.

Low iron is a common cause of tiredness, especially in people with heavy periods, in pregnancy, and in people who eat little iron-rich food, and a simple blood test can find it. Iron pills should not be taken unless a doctor advises it, Dev stresses, because too much iron can be harmful and the symptoms of low iron can have other causes. Priya says that she will make an appointment with her own doctor that very week, and she puts the bottle quietly back into her bag.

Vitamin B12 comes mainly from animal foods such as meat, fish, eggs and milk, and it is needed for healthy blood and nerves. People who eat none of these foods are usually advised to take fortified foods or a supplement, and anyone who suspects a lack should ask a doctor to test it and not guess. Dev adds that some medicines and some conditions of the gut also affect how well B12 is absorbed, which is another reason to ask a professional.

Sunlight helps the skin to make vitamin D, which is important for healthy bones and muscles, and a small amount comes from foods such as oily fish and eggs. In some countries, health authorities advise people to take a supplement during the darker months, when sunlight is weak, and Dev urges Hana to follow the advice of her own country. He does not tell her which dose to take, because that depends on the person and is a question for a doctor or a pharmacist.

Dev explains that vitamins do not give a person extra energy unless the body is short of them, and that taking more than the body needs rarely helps. A lack of vitamin B12 or vitamin D should be checked by a doctor with a blood test, not guessed at in a shop with a shiny label to guide the choice. Hana looks at the row of colourful jars with the cool eye of an expert.

Dev says that for most well-fed adults a multivitamin gives no proven boost to energy, and that the large tubs in the shops are mostly a matter of hope. Food is the better place to begin, he argues, because it also brings fibre, protein and many other good things that tablets cannot supply, but he would not forbid anyone from taking one if their doctor recommended it. Hana agrees that her money would be better spent on vegetables, and she promises to treat the tubs on the shelf as interesting but optional.

Hana reads a label that says that a vitamin supports normal energy metabolism, and she asks what that means in real life. It is not the same as giving you a boost, Dev explains, because it only describes what the vitamin does in a healthy body that already has enough of it. Hana says that shops should print that sentence in much larger letters on every jar, and Dev says that he would happily buy the pen.

Hana decides to book a routine visit to her doctor, just to be sure that nothing else is going on behind her tiredness. She does it at once on her phone, before she can find an excuse to wait, and the first free time is next Tuesday at nine. Dev says that he is glad, and that a diary is an excellent thing to bring along.

Hana stands at the whiteboard and summarises what she has learned so far, using plain words and a few clumsy drawings of a cell and a wave. Dev corrects only two small points and then tells her, with obvious sincerity, that she could easily be teaching the class. Marcus, who has come to look for a stapler, stays for the whole talk and takes notes.

Hana stretches her arms high above her head beside her desk, and she smiles at nobody in particular as her shoulders click. Regular exercise reduces tiredness in trials, Dev says, and even a short walk can raise alertness for a while, which is a pleasantly cheap form of medicine. He adds that this effect is one of the better supported ideas in their whole experiment.

Studies of people who feel tired show that regular, gentle exercise can improve energy levels over time, which sounds like a trick but is supported by the evidence. Even people who begin with very little activity seem to gain something, and they do not need to be athletes or to join an expensive gym. Hana, who has paid for three gyms and used none, finds this a great relief.

Health guides advise adults to aim for about 150 minutes of moderate activity each week, which sounds like a lot until it is divided into small pieces. It can be split into short sessions, and ten minutes at a time counts just as much, so a daily fifteen minute walk after lunch already covers a good part of it. Hana counts up her recent walks on her fingers and feels a warm and pleasant glow of quiet achievement.

Moderate activity means that you can talk comfortably but would find it hard to sing, Dev says, and that is a simple test that anyone can use. You do not need to run to feel the benefit, because a brisk walk is quite enough for most people, although people with health problems should ask a doctor what suits them. Hana tries to sing while walking and is told by a pigeon to stop.

Sitting for many hours is linked with poorer health, and the link remains even among people who exercise at other times of the day. Standing and moving every thirty to sixty minutes breaks up long sitting, Dev says, although nobody knows exactly what the best interval is, so he marks the exact timing as unknown. Hana looks at her office chair with deep suspicion and then, rather reluctantly, gets up and goes to fill her water bottle.

Hana now takes her phone calls on foot, with a headset round her neck, and she paces the corridor like a politician before an important speech. She also sets a gentle timer that reminds her to stand up and stretch every hour, and she discovers that a short break from the chair feels like a small holiday. Her colleagues begin to copy her, one by one, and soon the corridor becomes as crowded as a small and rather slow motorway.

Dev lifts a light weight in the park while Hana copies him with a heavy bag of shopping, which was all that she could find. Strength exercise builds muscle, which uses sugar from the blood, and guides advise strengthening activities at least twice a week for most adults, although the details depend on a person's health. Hana says that her arms already feel like cooked noodles and that this must be progress.

Hana joins Dev's evening running club at last, although she chooses the slow group at the back of the park, where nobody is in a hurry. They walk and jog gently in the dusk, chatting about television, and she is surprised by how much she enjoys it, and by how deeply she sleeps that night. She decides that being slow is perfectly respectable as long as one is still moving, and she looks forward to the next Thursday evening.

Too much exercise too soon can leave a person exhausted, sore and miserable, and it may even discourage them from ever going out again. Dev tells Hana to build up slowly, to rest between sessions, and to stop and see a doctor if she ever has chest pain, dizziness or unusual breathlessness during exercise. She promises to listen to her body and to wait for a signal before she gets carried away.

Hana colours three days of her diary yellow for movement, using a highlighter that she has borrowed from Priya. Her energy scores are highest on those days, although she notices that she also slept better on them, which makes it hard to say which of the two helped the other. Dev smiles and says that this is how real science feels, a little messy and very interesting.

Hana closes her eyes and puts a hand on her chest, where she can feel her heart beating a little faster than it should. Stress can tire the body and raise blood sugar, Dev says, and breathing slowly and taking short breaks may help, although no breath will rescue anyone from an impossible workload. Hana says that she would like the workload itself to hear that advice, and perhaps to take it to heart for a day or two.

A deadline week arrives with the speed of a train, and Hana's workload doubles overnight, with new figures to check and new reports to write. Her sleep, her walks and her steady lunches all disappear within two days, and the old slump returns with a vengeance, as if it had only been waiting outside. She writes in her diary that the experiment has been interrupted by real life.

Dev explains that in stress the body releases hormones, including one called cortisol, that raise blood sugar and keep us alert and ready to act. This is useful for a short time, such as when crossing a busy road, but it is tiring when it goes on for weeks, and it seems to leave many people feeling wired and flat at once. Hana says that this describes her week exactly, and she asks whether the body also comes with a manual for the weekend.

Dev teaches her to breathe in slowly for four counts and out even more slowly for six, with one hand on her stomach. Slow breathing may calm the body and lower the heart rate a little, he says, although the effect is modest and it is no cure for the problems that caused the stress in the first place. Hana practises it quietly under her desk for two minutes and feels slightly less like a wire.

Long periods of concentration use up mental energy, and the brain does not work well for hours on end without a rest. Hana takes a short break with a cup of tea and looks out of the office window at the trees and the clouds, and she is astonished at how quickly her mind begins to clear. Dev says that breaks are not a luxury but a part of the work itself.

Many people work well in blocks of about half an hour to an hour, with short breaks in between, and Hana sets a kitchen timer to try it. Dev says that there is no perfect rule and that research on the best length of block is not settled, so he asks her to find the rhythm that suits her own mind. After three days she settles on fifty minutes of work followed by ten minutes of walking.

Constant alerts and the habit of jumping between tasks drain attention and leave a person feeling that the day has been busy but empty, Dev says. Hana turns off her notifications for a part of every morning, and she finds that her work flows more easily and that nothing terrible happens to the world in the meantime. Priya says that she will believe it when she has tried it for a week.

Hana finds the courage to tell Marcus that the Tuesday meeting at three fifteen falls at her lowest point of the day, and she shows him a few honest lines from her diary. He listens in thoughtful silence and then agrees to move the meeting to eleven, since several other people in the team say that they are sharper in the morning too. Hana feels the quiet satisfaction of having asked for something reasonable, and of having been heard without a fight or an apology.

A dull task can feel far more tiring than a hard one, and Hana notices it every time that she has to fill in an expense form. Dev says that changing tasks, taking a brief walk and adding a small reward when the dull task is done can make it feel lighter, although he admits that the science of boredom is still young. Hana promises herself a mug of tea and five minutes of sunshine after every form that she completes, and she keeps her word.

If stress goes on for weeks, or if a person's mood stays low, it is sensible to talk to a doctor or to someone they trust. Dev says gently that asking for help is a sign of sense and never a sign of weakness, and that many people wait much too long before they speak. Hana's friend Nina sits with her on a bench in the park, listens, and says that she is not alone.

Alcohol can make people fall asleep faster, which is why a glass of wine in the evening feels like a friend. It harms the quality of sleep later in the night, however, and breaks it into lighter and more restless pieces, so evening drinks can lead to tired mornings even after a long night in bed. Dev says this without any judgement at all, as a plain and well-tested fact that comes from many careful studies.

On Friday evening Hana skips her usual glass of wine and compares her sleep with the week before, using her diary and a very honest memory. Dev says only that the choice is hers, and that he would never lecture her about it, since a sensible adult can read the evidence and decide without a sermon. She sleeps rather well, and she says that she will think about what that means.

Bright light at night can delay the body clock and make it harder to fall asleep, and the glow of a phone held close to the face is a typical culprit. Dimmer lights and less screen time in the last hour before bed may help, Dev says, although the size of the effect differs among people, and the content of what is on the screen may matter too. Hana switches off her tablet that evening and sits beside a lamp with a warm yellow glow, and she is surprised how pleasant the quiet is.

Hana builds a simple wind-down hour with warm light, a paperback book, a mug of herbal tea and absolutely no work. She begins to look forward to it with the pleasure of a child waiting for a story, and she wonders why nobody ever told her that adults are allowed to do this. Dev says that a routine, whatever its form, tells the body that sleep is on its way.

A cool, dark and quiet bedroom, together with a regular wake-up time, helps most people to sleep, because the body likes routine and responds to signals. Hana opens her window a little, hangs a heavy curtain, tidies the bed and puts on a clean sheet, and she discovers that the room already feels calmer and more welcoming. She says that she has never thought of her bedroom as an instrument before.

Hana decides to leave her phone to charge in the kitchen, far from her bedroom, and she buys a cheap alarm clock to replace it. She cannot scroll in bed any more, and at first she feels strangely lost, as if she has mislaid a limb, but within a week she feels only relief and a great deal more peace. Dev says that this may well be the most powerful change that she has made in the whole of the four weeks.

A short nap of about twenty minutes can improve alertness, Dev says, and Hana tries one on a park bench with a timer in her hand. Longer naps may leave a person groggy and slow, however, and a nap late in the day can harm sleep that night, so she keeps hers short and early. She wakes up feeling like a fresh sheet of paper and a little embarrassed by a passing jogger.

When her thoughts race at night, Hana writes tomorrow's list on a sheet of paper that she keeps beside her pillow, in a rather untidy hand. Many people find that putting worries on paper helps them to let go of them and fall asleep, although the research is limited and Dev calls the idea likely and not proven. For Hana, at least, it works very well, and she is happy to say so to anyone who asks her about her nights.

A warm bath taken an hour or two before bed may help some people to fall asleep, according to a number of studies, although the effect is small. The warmth is followed by a cooling of the body, which seems to tell the brain that it is time to rest, and Hana, who loves a good bath, takes the advice with enthusiasm. She emerges from the bathroom like a happy and slightly pink cat, and falls asleep before her book has even opened.

At the end of week three, Hana has slept for at least seven hours on five nights out of seven, which she writes in her diary in green ink. She feels a little more like her old self, and she has quietly stopped dreading the hour of three o'clock, although she does not yet dare to say that the dip has gone. Dev says that careful hope is precisely the right amount at this stage, and he writes the phrase on a sticky note for her.

Adrenal fatigue is not a recognised medical condition, and the products that promise to fix it have no good scientific evidence behind them. Real diseases of the adrenal glands do exist, but they are rare and need a doctor's tests and treatment, and a bottle from a shelf is no substitute for those. Dev labels the whole fashion unknown at best, and Hana puts a bottle labelled adrenal reset back where she found it.

The liver and the kidneys already clean the body all day long, Dev explains, and they do it far better than any pink tea from a shelf. There is no good evidence that detox teas or juice cleanses help, and some products, especially those with strong laxatives, can even cause harm, so Hana recalls her old cleanse with a shiver. She resolves to leave the cleaning to the organs that were built for it, and to spend her money on lentils instead.

Energy drinks combine caffeine and often a large amount of sugar, and they give a short boost that is followed by a drop. They are not advised for children, and some people feel jittery, anxious or unable to sleep after them, although tastes and reactions differ widely. Priya listens to Dev explain this with her can held rather protectively in both hands.

Priya reads the label of her energy drink with a puzzled face and discovers, with some shock, how much caffeine and sugar it contains. She decides to try water and tea for a week, as an experiment of her own, and she announces that she will report back to the team with graphs. Hana tells her that a notebook is the only scientific tool that she really needs.

Glucose monitors, which are small sensors worn on the skin, help people with diabetes to manage their condition and to treat it safely. For healthy people the benefit is unclear, because readings vary and a normal rise after a meal can look alarming on a graph, and the devices can cause needless worry and expense. Dev says that he would not advise a healthy person to buy one just for fun, and that a doctor should guide anyone with diabetes.

A colleague in the corridor proudly shows his phone, which displays a spiky graph, and he panics because it jumped after he ate a pear. Dev explains kindly that a rise in blood sugar after eating is normal in a healthy body, and that the line on the graph does not mean that something is wrong. The colleague looks hugely relieved and promises to stop tracking every single mouthful, and Hana notices that he already looks ten years younger.

Sleep trackers worn on the wrist give estimates of how long and how well a person sleeps, and these estimates can be wrong. They are not a medical test, Dev says, and some people become more anxious about their sleep when they check the numbers too often, which makes the sleep itself worse. Hana decides that she does not need a gadget to tell her how she feels.

Dev holds up three fingers and gives Hana three questions to ask of any claim that she meets on a shelf or a screen. What is the evidence, how big is the effect, and who is making money from selling it, he asks, and he says that a good claim survives all three without any trouble. Hana writes the questions on her hand and smiles at them like old friends.

A study that shows that two things are linked does not show that one causes the other, Dev says, and the difference is one of the most important ideas in science. A small study is also not a proof, and a single study is only a beginning, so a careful reader waits until several good studies point in the same direction before believing a bold headline. Hana says that she will try to be a careful reader from now on, and that she will start with the packaging of her own tea.

Hana pins a large board above her desk with three columns labelled proven, likely and unknown, and she sorts everything that she has learned so far into them. Morning light and sleep go into one column, walking after meals into another, and detox teas into a third, while Dev adds a few small corrections. She stands back and admires a map of what is known, and she feels more confident than she did a month ago.

Dev tells Hana that there is one lesson in their whole experiment that matters more than all the others, and he asks her to remember it. Tiredness that lasts for weeks, or comes with other signs such as low mood, breathlessness or weight loss, needs a doctor and not a diet or a diary. He says this firmly, because no list of habits can find a problem that only a proper examination can discover.

Dev writes a short list of warning signs on a red-edged card and hands it to Hana with a serious face. The signs include tiredness that lasts for weeks, extreme thirst, passing urine very often, blurred vision, unexplained weight loss, breathlessness and low mood that will not lift. Hana pins the card inside her wardrobe door, where she will see it every morning without being frightened.

Extreme thirst, passing urine very often, blurred vision, unexplained weight loss and unusual tiredness may be signs of diabetes, which is a condition in which the body cannot control its blood sugar properly. Anyone who notices them should see a doctor soon, who can test for it with a simple blood test and can arrange treatment, and nobody should try to diagnose it from a book. Hana nods gravely and writes down the date of her appointment, which she now intends to keep with great care.

Hana sits in the waiting room on Tuesday morning with her diary on her knee, feeling a little silly and a little nervous. The doctor reads it with real interest, asks about her sleep, her mood and her appetite, and orders a simple blood test to check for common causes of tiredness. Hana is grateful that nobody laughs at her notebook, and that nobody tells her that she is simply busy.

A few days later the test results come back normal, and the doctor says that Hana's steady habits are good ones to keep, since they support health in many ways. She leaves the clinic relieved and a little light-headed, and she realises that she had been worrying about a hidden illness for much longer than she had admitted. Dev says that a normal result is good news, but that it is not a reason to ignore a symptom that returns.

The doctor explains that long-lasting tiredness has many possible causes, such as low iron, a thyroid problem, a sleep disorder, an infection, a side effect of a medicine or low mood. Only an examination, a conversation and sometimes tests can tell them apart, she says, and that is exactly why guessing from a magazine is a poor way to solve the puzzle. Hana says that she has already stopped guessing and that she would far rather ask a person who has studied for years.

Dev tells Hana about his aunt Ruth, who lives with a long illness that makes her tired every single day, however well she sleeps or eats. No diet or morning walk would be a fair cure for her, and he says that people like her deserve patience, understanding and good medical care, and never a lecture about willpower. Hana listens with a lump in her throat and says that she understands, and she asks Dev to give his aunt her warmest wishes.

Hana's sister Leila has a newborn baby and sleeps only in broken pieces, which is nobody's fault and which no schedule can quite repair. Dev says that she should accept all the help that she is offered, rest when the baby rests, and ask her doctor or midwife for advice if she feels truly overwhelmed. Hana takes round a pot of lentil soup and does the washing up, and Leila looks as if she might cry with relief.

Some medicines cause drowsiness as a side effect, Dev says, and that is a good reason to read the leaflet and to ask a doctor or a pharmacist about it. People should never stop a medicine by themselves because of a tired feeling, since stopping suddenly can be harmful, and the right answer may be a different dose or a different time of day. Hana makes a note to tell everyone she knows, beginning with Priya, who has a medicine cabinet the size of a small pharmacy.

Tiredness and low mood often come together, and it can be hard to tell which one began first, which is why a doctor can help with both. Dev says that effective treatment exists, that many people recover, and that talking to a doctor or a trusted person is a brave and sensible step and never a failure. Hana sits beside him on a bench, quietly drinking her tea, and feels grateful for his honesty.

Hana sits on a bench in the park and reads her diary from the very first page, with a small smile that she cannot quite hide. Her best days follow good sleep and a walk, and her worst days follow a short night and a skipped lunch, and she circles that line with the pen that she has carried for a month. The pattern is not dramatic or surprising, but it is hers, and it was found with her own pen, in her own life.

Hana lays four weeks of diary pages out across the table in the break room and studies them with the concentration of a detective. The scores show a clear pattern, with sleep, a walk and regular meals standing far ahead of coffee timing, breakfast choice and everything else, although the sample is only one person. Dev examines them with equal care, nods in agreement, and then adds that the pattern fits what research would lead anyone to expect.

Hana spends Saturday afternoon on a picnic blanket in the park with her friends Nina and Sam, laughing until her sides ache. Time with friends and doing things that matter to us also support energy and mood, Dev says, although they are hard to measure and do not fit neatly into any column of her diary. Hana says that she will give friends and fun a column of their own in the diary, and she writes the heading in bright blue ink.

After four weeks, Hana's afternoons are noticeably better but they are not perfect, and the dip at three still arrives, only smaller and kinder. Dev says that this is normal, that the body clock never completely disappears, and that one person's result is not proof for anyone else. They stand together on the office steps at dusk, tired and satisfied after a busy day.

Dev draws a bank account on the whiteboard, with deposits labelled sleep, food, movement and rest, and with a few withdrawals labelled stress and late nights. Energy is rather like a bank account, he says, because regular small deposits matter more than one huge payment, and no single deposit can cover every bill that life sends. Hana says that she finally understands why her account was always overdrawn, and that she has been spending far more than she was saving.

Hana writes five habits on a bright card and pins it to her fridge door, where she will see it every time she reaches for the milk. They are morning light, a regular bedtime, a steady lunch, a walk after eating and coffee before noon, and not one of them requires a special product or a lot of money. She feels that she could live with this list for ever, and that perhaps, for the first time, a plan has fitted her life.

Hana throws her old miracle teas and her half-empty tablet bottles into the bin with a certain ceremony, like a pirate dropping a map into the sea. She throws away her guilt at the same time, and she says that a bad afternoon is no longer a personal failure but simply the body clock having its say. Dev applauds quietly, and Priya, who has been watching from her desk with a bottle of water, applauds loudly and then whistles.

Priya joins the lunchtime walk after her week of water and tea, and she reports, with graphs, that her afternoons have improved. Soon half the team goes out with them in the thin autumn sunshine, and Marcus begins to walk too, admitting that his meetings are shorter and his temper is milder. Hana looks at the little crowd and wonders when an experiment becomes a culture.

Hana knows that her habits helped her, but she also knows that she was fortunate to have a body that responded so well and a job that allowed her to walk at lunch. People with long-term conditions, shift work or small children may find the same habits impossible, and they deserve kindness and a doctor's help and never blame or quick fixes. She tucks that thought safely into the back of her notebook, where she will be able to find it whenever she feels too pleased with herself.

That evening, Hana and Dev sit on a bench with two cups of tea and agree that steady energy comes from many small habits, such as sleep, light, regular meals, movement and calm, and not from any single trick. This book gives general information only and is not medical advice, so anyone with a health condition, diabetes, a pregnancy, a child to feed or a medicine to take should ask a doctor first. For everyone else, the next step is small and cheap, which is to take a ten-minute walk after your next meal.
